newsitem.title: UK: Fed in focus, but some see ominous signs for G3.
newsitem.headline: Fed in focus, but some see ominous signs for G3.

text.p: Speculation about a move in U.S. interest rates next week is at fever pitch but some analysts are far more concerned about what will happen next year.

And they're not just looking at the U.S. but also at the other two Group of Three (G3) members -- Japan and Germany. Bond markets in all three countries have come under pressure and some say the idea of tighter credit is the reason.
Tom Hobson, director of technical analysis at Merrill Lynch in London, said charts of 1998 contracts for U.S., Japanese and German interest rate futures had all suffered lately.
"The breakdowns recently have decidedly indicated the bland tone that has dominated markets has been halted," Hobson said.

Markets are edgy about the thought that the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), the Federal Reserve's policy arm, not only will tighten credit at a meeting on March 25 but also will kick off a series of rises into the second half of next year.

This, analysts said, could come as Japan's battered financial sector begins to find its feet, allowing currently paltry Japanese interest rates to rise, and as Germany's economy begins to recover, allowing German rates to perk up too.
"Bonds are suffering partly because people are taking on board the fact that, like it or not, world growth is accelerating," said Peter Von Maydell senior currency economist at UBS in London.
For Merrill's Hobson, the signs are in the futures markets.

For instance, the June 1998 contract for Eurodollars is currently trading at 93.42, reflecting market expectations that three-month U.S. interest rates will be nearly 6.60 percent by the time the contract expires. That compares with current three-month money rates of 5.15 percent.
More importantly, the June 1998 Eurodollars have been trending lower and are sitting on critical support levels. The lower they go, the higher people think interest rates will be.

Meanwhile, June 1998 Euromarks -- the equivalent contract for German interest rates -- are also at an important technical juncture. They were quoted at 93.95 and have been hovering above the 93.90-91 area recently, an area of support which has shored up the market on numerous occasions since mid-December.

The biggest movement in interest rate futures has been in the place with the lowest rates. Japanese June 1998 Euroyen futures tumbled 18 basis points from a 98.92 high on Tuesday to a 98.74 low on Wednesday.
All of this is adding to bond market worries, analysts said.
"I don't anticipate the markets giving up everything they've achieved. But the risk is definitely to the downside in the next one to two months," Hobson said.
But looking beyond the immediate horizon, there is a wide range of thoughts about interest rates, especially in the U.S.

Dick Howard, senior economist at Julius Baer Investments, said some are looking for the Fed to nudge up rates gently, perhaps two or three times by a quarter percentage point each during the next nine months. Others think at least 1.25 percentage points of tightening is needed.
"The world seems to be divided into two camps," he said.
While he favoured the less aggressive scenario there, in Japan Howard said there was a risk of rates rising 100 to 150 basis points once the Bank of Japan decides to start moving.
Japan, he said, might be in a similar position to the U.S., which had low interest rates for a long period in the early part of this decade, then endured a number of tightenings in 1994.
Howard was least concerned about German rates.

"We think there's a healthy pickup in economic activity ahead over the spring and summer but we don't think there will be any problems on the inflation front to speak of, so we don't think the Bundesbank is going to move rates before early next year," he said.
"We sure are at the bottom of the interest rate cycle but I think Germany may be the laggard in its interest rate tightening."
